title: Bidets: Now More Than Ever
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss bidets during the early COVID-19 toilet paper shortage. They cover the bidet's origins as a seventeenth-century French bedroom device (the name meaning pony or cob horse), its spread across Europe and Asia, why America resisted it (anti-French sentiment, association with brothels seen by WWII soldiers, taboo around menstruation, bathroom size), Arnold Cohen's 1960s American Bidet design, Toto's washlet and its sales, the three main bidet types, how to use one, medical benefits and a Japanese study linking warm-water bidets to vaginal flora disruption, and the environmental cost of toilet paper. The episode ends with listener mail about a license plate reading 666 mph.

segments.title: Opening banter and COVID toilet paper context
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show and Jerry, then discuss how bidets help during the toilet paper rush, with Chuck disliking toilet paper for wiping and Josh using a little paper after a bidet.

segments.title: Origins of the bidet in 17th-18th century France
segments.summary: The name bidet means pony or cob horse. Early bidets were low basins used in bedrooms next to chamber pots, mostly by the upper class who had servants to haul water. Christophe de Rosier is credited with making one for the French royal family. A hand pump spray came around the 1750s, followed by a refillable tank. Italy and Portugal adopted them, and the French popularized them.

segments.title: Lou etymology digression
segments.summary: Josh shares a tour-guide explanation from Edinburgh that the British word lou for toilet may derive from the Scottish shout 'guardiloo', from French 'guarde de l'eau'.

segments.title: Why America never adopted the bidet
segments.summary: Hosts cite a bidet expert's theories: English hatred of France carried into the colonies, American soldiers seeing bidets in brothels during World War II, bidets' association with sex work and douching as contraception, and taboo around menstruation. They also discuss whether bathrooms shrank because bidets were absent.

segments.title: Arnold Cohen and the American Bidet
segments.summary: Arnold Cohen, a former ad man, designed a bidet in the 1960s for his aging father with rectal problems. His American Sitz Bath attached to a toilet seat with a foot pump. He was driven partly by toilet paper consumption. He licensed the concept to Toto, which made it electronic and automated and introduced the washlet in Japan.

segments.title: Bidet types and washlet sales
segments.summary: Hosts discuss cheap bidet seat attachments (around thirty to fifty dollars, cold water), high-end washlets with heated seats and dryers, and the need for an electrical outlet. Washlet sales reached seventeen million by 2007, fifty million by 2019. Hosts name the three bidet types: standalone basin, seat attachment, and wall-mounted handheld hose.

segments.title: Sponsor break and bidet use steps
segments.summary: A break is taken. Afterward the hosts walk through how to use a bidet: use the toilet, spray, then dry with a little toilet paper or air dry or use a dryer. They also discuss sitting on the toilet too long and not watching TV in bed.

segments.title: Medical uses of bidets and UTI concerns
segments.summary: Doctors and specialists may recommend bidets for colitis, IBS, Crohn's, colon cancer, hemorrhoids, fissures, and itchy anus. Bidets may help elderly or arthritic people stay independent. Bidets may help reduce UTIs when used before and after sex. A Japanese study of 268 women linked warm-water bidet use to disrupted vaginal microflora and more fecal bacteria.

segments.title: Toilet paper environmental cost
segments.summary: Americans use a large share of the world's toilet paper, much of it from old-growth Canadian boreal forests, described as the tree-to-toilet pipeline. Americans use about forty rolls a year per person and households about a hundred and fifty. Bidets use far less paper and water efficiently.

segments.title: Mike's Mighty Good Ramen mention and bidet recommendation
segments.summary: Hosts thank Mike's Mighty Good Ramen for sending free product and describe eating it, and Josh recommends Toto washlets.

segments.title: Listener mail: 666 license plate
segments.summary: Mary Kerr of Buffalo, New York, writes about her brother Matt who moved to Wisconsin and was offered the plate number 666 mph by a DMV employee, then chose a different number. The hosts close with the show sign-off.
